# INTRODUCTION

This chapter identifies the problem that the study addresses and defines the objectives of a solution. It describes why the problem matters, what the study asks and aims to achieve, the frameworks behind the study, and the boundaries and significance of the study.

## Introduction to the Study

According to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration [PAGASA, -@pagasa2026cyclone], about eight or nine tropical cyclones cross the Philippines each year. During these events, Filipinos use social media to warn others, report damage, and ask for help [@ermino2022urgency; @caoile2025urdaneta]. However, the sheer volume of posts makes useful information difficult and time-consuming for responders to find [@somido2023actionable]. Natural language processing (NLP) can help automate this work [@lewis2025tapping]. Specifically, humanitarian classification assigns each post a category by report type [@alam2021humaid], while named entity recognition (NER) identifies details such as affected locations and requests for aid [@ali2026humaidner].

A multi-task model trained on both tasks simultaneously can outperform separate single-task models, as representations learned for one task can inform the other [@wang2021transformer]. However, learning one task can also interfere with learning the other, a problem known as negative transfer [@royer2023scalarization]. Multi-task optimizers aim to reduce this problem by balancing how tasks influence the shared model during training [@xin2022mtohelp]. Yet studies disagree on whether specialized multi-task optimizers (SMTOs) outperform equal weighting, which assigns both tasks the same weight [@gama2026uniform]. Many SMTOs also take longer to train than equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary; @xin2022mtohelp].

Although code-switching between Tagalog and English, known as Taglish, is widespread in the Philippines [@herrera2022tweettaglish], none of the studies reviewed provides a dataset where the same Taglish posts are annotated for both tasks or benchmarks multi-task optimizers on such data. This study addresses these gaps by building an annotated dataset of Taglish typhoon posts and benchmarking 13 multi-task optimizers on negative transfer and training cost. The final model uses the optimizer selected from this benchmark and is evaluated against single-task baselines. The study contributes the dataset, the final model, and evidence on how much these optimizers reduce negative transfer and at what training cost.

## Background of the Study

The Philippines faces the highest disaster risk among 193 countries, partly because of its high exposure to weather-related extremes [@bundnis2025worldriskreport]. During disasters, social media posts provide responders with firsthand information from affected communities, but the sheer volume of posts makes finding actionable details time-consuming [@somido2023actionable]. Researchers have turned to NLP to automate this process by classifying posts and extracting key information [@mcdaniel2024zeroshot]. In this context, humanitarian classification identifies the type of report, while NER identifies details such as locations and requests for aid [@ali2026humaidner].

Several Philippine studies have applied NLP to disaster posts. For classification, @ermino2022urgency categorized typhoon posts by urgency, while @somido2023actionable identified informative disaster posts. For extraction, @yute2021satellite applied NER to extract location names from posts about the 2020 Taal Volcano eruption. More recently, @caoile2025urdaneta used a large language model (LLM) to extract place names and detect sentiment, urgency, and intent in Facebook comments. However, each of these studies either trained a model for a single task or relied on an LLM instead of a trained model.

A multi-task model could provide both kinds of information at the same time. It shares one pretrained transformer encoder between the tasks and gives each task its own task head, the part of the model that makes the predictions for that task [@wang2021transformer; @gama2026uniform]. Because the encoder already captures general language representations from pretraining, it can be fine-tuned effectively on a relatively small dataset annotated for both tasks [@bucher2024finetuned].

However, multi-task models can also perform worse on a task than single-task models, a problem known as negative transfer [@kurin2022unitary; @royer2023scalarization]. This drop in performance has been reported when classification and NER are trained together. In @zhu2025prefinetuning, an encoder trained on both tasks performed slightly worse than single-task baselines because the two tasks pulled token representations in conflicting directions. Similarly, @ali2026humaidner found that classification performance declined during joint training, which the authors attributed to an imbalance, as NER provides a training signal for every token while classification provides only one signal for the entire post.

Studies disagree on whether SMTOs reduce negative transfer better than equal weighting. SMTOs adjust how strongly each task influences the model as training proceeds, whereas equal weighting keeps both task weights identical throughout training [@gama2026uniform]. When evaluated against equal weighting [@kurin2022unitary] or well-tuned fixed weights [@xin2022mtohelp], SMTOs often showed no performance advantage, despite the extra training time and memory that many of them need. Conversely, @gama2026uniform found that SMTOs matched equal weighting on two similar tasks but outperformed it on more complex problems.

These studies leave two research gaps. First, none of the studies reviewed provides Taglish posts annotated for both humanitarian classification and NER. Evaluating both outputs of a multi-task model requires posts annotated for both tasks. While @ali2026humaidner built such a dataset for English by adding NER spans to existing HumAID posts [@alam2021humaid], Tagalog and Taglish remain low-resource languages with a shortage of annotated datasets [@cruz2022tagalog; @herrera2022tweettaglish]. Second, none of the studies reviewed compares multi-task optimizers for humanitarian classification and NER on Taglish posts, on either negative transfer or training cost. Because the performance of multi-task optimizers depends on the problem [@gama2026uniform], the optimizer that best reduces negative transfer cannot be known in advance and must be determined through an empirical benchmark.

## Statement of the Problem

This study aims to develop a dataset and a multi-task model for humanitarian classification and NER of Taglish typhoon posts, and to compare multi-task optimizers for this model in negative transfer and training cost. Specifically, it answers four research questions.

1. What F1-scores do single-task models achieve for humanitarian classification and for NER on Taglish typhoon posts? (Baseline Analysis)

2. How can a dataset and a multi-task model be designed for humanitarian classification and NER of Taglish typhoon posts? (Design and Artifact Creation)

3. How do the 13 multi-task optimizers compare in negative transfer, training time, and peak memory? (Empirical Benchmarking)

4. How does the final multi-task model compare with the single-task models in F1-score, training time, and peak memory? (Comparative Validation)

## Objectives

The general objective is to develop a dataset and a multi-task model for humanitarian classification and NER of Taglish typhoon posts, and to compare multi-task optimizers for this model in negative transfer and training cost. Specifically, the study pursues four objectives.

1. To measure the F1-scores of single-task models for humanitarian classification and for NER on Taglish typhoon posts. (Baseline Analysis)

2. To design and build a dataset and a multi-task model for humanitarian classification and NER of Taglish typhoon posts. (Design and Artifact Creation)

3. To compare the 13 multi-task optimizers in negative transfer, training time, and peak memory. (Empirical Benchmarking)

4. To compare the final multi-task model with the single-task models in F1-score, training time, and peak memory. (Comparative Validation)

## Hypotheses

The study tests the following null and alternative hypotheses for each of the two tasks, humanitarian classification and NER.

**Null hypothesis ($H_0$).** The mean F1-score across training runs of the final multi-task model is the same as that of the single-task model for that task.

**Alternative hypothesis ($H_1$).** The mean F1-score across training runs of the final multi-task model differs from that of the single-task model for that task.

## Theoretical Framework

This study is grounded in the theory of multi-task learning as inductive transfer [@caruana1997multitask]. Under this framework, related tasks share an underlying representation, allowing knowledge from one task to inform the others. Positive transfer occurs when learning the tasks together improves performance on a task, whereas negative transfer occurs when learning one task interferes with learning the other [@royer2023scalarization]. While multi-task models outperform single-task baselines in some studies [@wang2021transformer], they suffer from negative transfer and perform worse in others [@zhu2025prefinetuning]. Because both tasks share a pretrained transformer encoder, the final multi-task model may show either positive or negative transfer on each task. The hypotheses therefore test for a difference in F1-score in either direction.

## Conceptual Framework

The conceptual framework of this study consists of the research paradigm in @fig-research-paradigm and the design of the multi-task model in @fig-artifact. It centers on two comparisons, one among the 13 multi-task optimizers and one between the final multi-task model and the single-task models.

![Research Paradigm](figures/fig-1-1-research-paradigm.pdf){#fig-research-paradigm}

@fig-research-paradigm follows the Input-Process-Output (IPO) model. The inputs are the Taglish posts, the categories of HumAID and the entity types of HUMAID-NER, the pretrained transformer encoder, the 13 multi-task optimizers, and the laptop used for training. The process has four steps, each answering one research question. The study first designs and builds the dataset and the multi-task model (RQ2), then trains a single-task model for each task to measure baseline F1-scores (RQ1). It then benchmarks the 13 multi-task optimizers and selects the optimizer of the final model based on negative transfer (RQ3). Finally, it compares the final model with the single-task models (RQ4). The outputs are the dataset, the final multi-task model, and the comparison of the 13 multi-task optimizers.

![Multi-Task Model](figures/fig-1-2-artifact.pdf){#fig-artifact}

@fig-artifact shows how the multi-task model processes an example post. Both tasks share one pretrained transformer encoder, which processes the post in a single pass. The classification head uses the output for the whole post and assigns it a humanitarian category, while the NER head uses the output for each token and identifies the named entities. The dashed lines show the steps that occur only during training, in which the multi-task optimizer combines the losses, the measures of how far the predictions of the model are from the correct labels, or the gradients of both tasks to update the shared encoder so that the model improves on both tasks.

## Scope, Limitations, and Delimitations

### Scope of the Study

The dataset covers Taglish posts on X, formerly Twitter, about the tropical cyclones of January to November 2026. The posts come from one day before to three days after each tropical cyclone was within the Philippine Area of Responsibility, the area that PAGASA monitors for tropical cyclones, based on the dates in the preliminary reports of PAGASA [-@pagasa2026prelim]. It consists of about 2,500 posts, each annotated with one of the ten humanitarian categories of HumAID [@alam2021humaid] and the ten entity types of HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner].

Two single-task models are trained, one for each task, alongside a multi-task model that performs both tasks. All models are built on one pretrained transformer encoder, SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, which was trained on 13 languages, including English and Filipino [@aisingapore2026sealion]. The multi-task model shares this encoder between the two tasks and is trained with each of the 13 multi-task optimizers reviewed in Section 2.2, which gives 13 candidate models from which the final model is selected based on negative transfer.

The study measures inter-annotator agreement on the humanitarian categories, as well as the F1-score on each task, the training time, and the peak memory for every model. The final model is then integrated into a prototype web application that performs humanitarian classification and NER, with functional tests verifying each of its features.

### Limitations of the Study

The dataset may not fully represent all Taglish posts about tropical cyclones, and automatic entity annotations may contain errors. The posts come only from users of X, who may not represent everyone affected by tropical cyclones. X also does not reliably show the region of a user, so the dataset may not represent the Taglish of every region equally. The size of about 2,500 posts is set by annotation capacity rather than by what the models need, so the dataset may be too small, and Section 3.7 checks whether it is large enough with a learning curve. The keywords cover only the roots *bagyo* and *baha* and the words formed from them, so posts about a tropical cyclone that use neither, such as a request for rescue that mentions only submerged houses, fall outside the dataset. Posts that name the tropical cyclone or flooding may therefore be overrepresented, and humanitarian categories whose posts rarely use these words may have few posts. Rare humanitarian categories may also have too few test posts for precise F1-scores. The entity spans are annotated automatically by GLiNER and are not checked by the annotators (Section 3.4), so the F1-scores for NER measure agreement with these annotations rather than with human annotations. For the humanitarian categories, disagreements unresolved by discussion are decided by a single adjudicator without independent verification.

The experiments are limited by the number of training runs and by the laptop used for training. Each model is trained only five times, so the comparison of the 13 optimizers is descriptive, and small differences between them may reflect the random seeds rather than the optimizers. With only five pairs of runs, the paired t-tests may also fail to detect a small difference between the final model and a single-task model. The training time and peak memory may differ on computers other than the laptop used. The F1-scores may also be lower than if every layer of the encoder were trained, because the embedding layer is frozen to fit the 8 GB of GPU memory of the laptop (Section 3.5).

The findings reflect tropical cyclones from January to November 2026 and may not generalize to storm seasons in other years. The comparison of the optimizers is based on one pair of tasks and one pretrained transformer encoder. Because the findings on multi-task optimizers depend on the problem [@gama2026uniform], the best optimizer may differ for other tasks or encoders.

### Delimitations of the Study

The dataset covers only Taglish posts on X about the tropical cyclones of January to November 2026. Platforms other than X are omitted. X allows posts collected through its API to be stored provided that posts deleted on the platform are also removed [@x2026devpolicy], and earlier disaster datasets similarly rely on Twitter data [@ermino2022urgency; @somido2023actionable; @alam2021humaid]. Other Philippine languages, such as Cebuano and Waray, are omitted, as mixing languages would obscure whether the model performs consistently in each language. The study focuses solely on tropical cyclones, excluding other natural hazards such as earthquakes and volcanic eruptions, because cyclones alone cross the Philippines eight to nine times a year [PAGASA, -@pagasa2026cyclone] which gives several events in a single year. Data from earlier years is omitted because model training depends on total annotated posts rather than a multi-year historical span, and the study does not analyze linguistic shifts over time. December 2026 is excluded because data collection must end before annotation begins that month. Non-text media such as images, video, and audio are excluded because both target tasks operate strictly on text.

The study restricts its scope to humanitarian classification and NER. Additional tasks, such as sentiment analysis, urgency detection, and hazard classification, are set aside because extra tasks would change how the tasks interfere with one another, making differences in negative transfer harder to attribute to the optimizers. Consequently, the model does not score urgency levels or identify specific hazard types. It also does not translate posts into English, since the shared encoder is pretrained on both English and Filipino [@aisingapore2026sealion]. Verifying the truthfulness of posts is omitted because confirming claims requires external sources such as official reports.

The empirical benchmark evaluates 13 existing multi-task optimizers using one shared encoder on a single laptop. Rather than developing a novel optimizer, the study focuses on evaluating established methods, and other existing optimizers are omitted to keep the total number of training runs feasible. Alternative encoders are omitted to avoid introducing confounding variables. Other computers are excluded so that training time and peak memory are measured under the same conditions. Evaluations are conducted solely on the test posts collected for this study, as external benchmarks such as HUMAID-NER [@ali2026humaidner] differ in language and annotation schemes. Finally, the model is not compared with LLMs, such as GPT, which differ in size, training, and deployment cost. Earlier studies have already made this comparison for text classification [@bucher2024finetuned], including disaster posts [@mcdaniel2024zeroshot].

The study does not evaluate operational deployment or live field use. Deployments during actual disasters and formal usability evaluations with local disaster risk reduction and management staff are omitted, as the research objectives center on building the dataset and the model and on benchmarking the optimizers. Ongoing software maintenance is outside the scope of the study. Instead, the final model, source code, and dataset post IDs are published on GitHub to allow future researchers to retrain and adapt the model for new events.

## Significance of the Study

This study mainly benefits researchers in NLP and in crisis informatics, the field that examines how social media information can support disaster response. These researchers gain a dataset of Taglish typhoon posts annotated for both humanitarian classification and NER, which none of the studies reviewed provides, to train and evaluate models for both tasks.

For researchers in multi-task learning, the study provides empirical evidence on how effectively SMTOs mitigate negative transfer compared with equal weighting, alongside their computational costs. Because the superiority of SMTOs remains contested across tasks and benchmarks [@kurin2022unitary; @xin2022mtohelp; @gama2026uniform], these findings offer new evidence from a low-resource, code-switched linguistic setting.

For local disaster risk reduction and management offices, the study provides a proof of concept demonstrating how a single model can classify incoming posts and extract key entities simultaneously. The comparative evaluation clarifies the performance trade-offs of using one multi-task model rather than maintaining two separate single-task models, while the prototype illustrates how emergency personnel could identify urgent rescue and relief requests more rapidly during disasters.

Future researchers can extend this work through the public release of the trained model, source code, annotation guidelines, and dataset post IDs on GitHub. This open access enables others to retrain the model on future tropical cyclones, build similar datasets for other Philippine languages, or integrate additional disaster response tasks such as urgency detection.

## Definitions of Terms

The following terms are defined as they are used in this study.

**Candidate model:** One of the 13 multi-task models, each trained with a different multi-task optimizer, from which the final model is selected.

**Equal weighting:** The multi-task optimizer that adds the losses of the tasks with the same weight throughout training [@kurin2022unitary]. In this study, the training cost of the other 12 optimizers is measured against it.

**F1-score:** A metric from 0 to 1 calculated as the harmonic mean of precision, the proportion of predictions that are correct, and recall, the proportion of true instances correctly identified. In this study, humanitarian classification is scored with macro-F1, the mean of the F1-scores of all categories, and NER with span-level micro-F1, which counts an entity as correct only when both its boundaries and its type match the annotation [@ali2026humaidner].

**Final model:** The candidate model trained with the multi-task optimizer selected based on negative transfer, which is compared with the single-task models.

**Humanitarian classification:** The task of assigning a post one category that names the kind of humanitarian information it reports [@alam2021humaid]. In this study, each post receives one of the ten categories of HumAID, such as requests or urgent needs.

**Inter-annotator agreement:** The degree to which annotators who annotate the same items independently give the same annotations. In this study, it is measured with Cohen's kappa between the two annotators on the humanitarian categories [@cohen1960coefficient].

**Loss:** A measure of how far the predictions of a model are from the correct labels, which training seeks to reduce. In this study, each task has a cross-entropy loss, and the multi-task optimizer combines the losses of the two tasks or their gradients.

**Multi-task model:** A model trained on several tasks together that shares a representation across them [@caruana1997multitask]. In this study, it is one pretrained transformer encoder shared by a task head for humanitarian classification and a task head for NER.

**Multi-task optimizer:** An algorithm that combines task losses or task gradients into a single parameter update for a shared multi-task model [@lin2023libmtl]. The study compares 13 multi-task optimizers.

**Named entity recognition (NER):** The task of finding the words or phrases in a text that name specific details and assigning each an entity type. In this study, the posts are annotated with the ten entity types of HUMAID-NER, such as locations and requests [@ali2026humaidner].

**Negative transfer:** A drop in performance on a task when it is trained together with another task, compared with training it alone [@royer2023scalarization]. In this study, it is a lower F1-score of a candidate model on a task than that of the single-task model for that task, and a higher F1-score is positive transfer.

**Peak memory:** The largest amount of GPU memory allocated during one training run.

**Post:** A message published on social media. In this study, it is a public post on X, which the title calls a Tweet, the name used when X was called Twitter.

**Pretrained transformer encoder:** A language model trained on large amounts of text before it is used for a task, which converts text tokens into numerical vectors for task heads. In this study, it is SEA-LION-ModernBERT-300M, which was trained on 13 languages, including English and Filipino [@aisingapore2026sealion].

**Single-task model:** A model trained on one task only. In this study, each single-task model uses the same pretrained transformer encoder as the multi-task model with one task head, and its F1-score is the baseline for measuring negative transfer on that task.

**Specialized multi-task optimizer (SMTO):** A multi-task optimizer that adjusts how strongly each task influences the model as training proceeds [@gama2026uniform]. In this study, these are the 11 of the 13 optimizers that do not keep the task weights fixed.

**Taglish:** Code-switching between Tagalog and English in the same text [@herrera2022tweettaglish]. In this study, a post is Taglish when it has at least one English word and one Tagalog word.

**Task head:** The part of a multi-task or single-task model that makes the predictions for one task from the output of the pretrained transformer encoder.

**Token:** A word or part of a word that the pretrained transformer encoder reads as one unit.

**Training cost:** The training time and peak memory of a model. Training time is the wall-clock time of the training steps of one run.

**Typhoon:** In the title, any tropical cyclone, a rotating storm that forms over warm ocean water. In this study, it covers all tropical cyclones that entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility from January to November 2026.
